thema_eingabe: WeWork: Gruendung, Expansion und die Folgen des Wachstums

skript.thema: WeWork: Gruendung, Expansion und die Folgen des Wachstums

teile.name: Hook
teile.text: WeWork's valuation once hit $47 billion. Then came bankruptcy. It started with one rented SoHo location.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: a man in a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch stands before a SoHo cast-iron loft building at dusk, warm window light, medium wide shot, calm sky above.

teile.name: Gruendung
teile.text: Adam Neumann and Miguel McKelvey sold their Brooklyn coworking space. In 2010, they founded WeWork.
teile.szene: Painted urban poster style: two anonymous illustrative men shake hands inside a bright Brooklyn shared workspace with plants and wooden desks, late afternoon light, medium shot, not real-person likenesses.

teile.name: Wachstum
teile.text: By 2013, 350 startups were customers. By 2014, it was New York's fastest-growing lessee of new office space.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game style: a busy open-plan office with small startup teams at long shared desks, notebooks and coffee cups in focus, warm overhead light, wide shot, calm ceiling area.

teile.name: Geld
teile.text: The money poured in. Over ten years, it raised $12.8 billion, mostly from SoftBank's Vision Fund.
teile.szene: Painted poster style: stacks of banknotes on a polished boardroom table overlooking a glowing city skyline at night, close-up with cool blue light, empty space above and below.

teile.name: Zukaeufe
teile.text: It kept buying: a coding school, Meetup, even a private school for children. Meetup was sold at a loss.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: split view of a small children's classroom with colorful desks on one side and adults working at a workshop table on the other, soft daylight, medium wide shot.

teile.name: Leck
teile.text: Trouble showed early. In 2016, WeWork fired and sued an employee who leaked that it would miss its financial goals.
teile.szene: Painted urban poster style: an employee carries a cardboard box past glass meeting-room walls in a quiet office, tense cool lighting, medium shot, figure centered, calm top and bottom.

teile.name: Wendung
teile.text: In September 2019, WeWork filed to go public. The filing revealed corporate governance issues. Investors forced the IPO's cancellation and Neumann's resignation.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: serious investors in suits around a long boardroom table, one empty leather chair at the head, dramatic side light from tall windows, medium wide shot.

teile.name: Insolvenz
teile.text: It went public through a SPAC merger in 2021 instead. Then it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on November 6, 2023.
teile.szene: Painted urban poster style: the fedora-wearing presenter in grey suit stands before a grand courthouse entrance in grey morning light, wide shot, calm sky above, gold pocket watch glinting.

teile.name: Aufloesung
teile.text: But it didn't vanish. It sold all its owned real estate and cancelled or amended hundreds of leases. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: a ring of keys and a stack of lease papers on an empty office desk beside a large window at sunset, warm restrained light, close shot, calm areas above and below.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

For AI Tools Explained Shorts comparable to the approved 82-second pilot, aim for 14-18 distinct relevant motifs instead of the previous 12 across 23 shots. Reduce repeated identical imagery and add genuinely different demonstrations, details or illustrative actions supported by the narration. Zooms, crops and label changes do not count as new motifs. This is a planning target, not a retroactive rejection of the positively received pilot.

For Business Origin Stories the user's latest refinement on 2026-10-05 is to aim for about 24 shots with 18 distinct relevant motifs for comparable 90-second Shorts. The delivered 24-shot/14-motif video was positively received; 18 motifs is the next improvement target, not its actual delivered count. Reduce repeats by adding four genuinely different relevant subjects or actions. Preserve useful pacing and the original channel character. Do not count zooms, crops or label changes as new motifs; adapt other video lengths to their story.
Explicit viewer feedback about our videos (not source facts): Es wurden einfach viel zu wenig Fotos verwendet
Start every video with a highly visual, specific, and engaging hook with immediate stakes without giving away the core twist or relying on vague academic setups.

Ensure every single scene features dynamic, contextually accurate visual clips or animations that strictly match the specific subject matter without using metaphorical or mismatched imagery like gardening tools for corporate growth.
Eliminate generic business history phrasing and chronological filler like 'Growth happened fast' to maintain constant narrative tension and a fast-paced story.
Eliminate historical dates, exact employee counts, names, and chronological transitions like 'In [Year]' to maintain a fast-paced story rather than a textbook timeline.
Eliminate corporate jargon, technical financial figures, and biographical filler to maintain high retention.
Replace generic narrative transitions with engaging, specific hooks that sustain momentum through the middle section.
Omit serial markers like Part 1 or Part 2 from the text and screen to avoid confusing viewers in short-form videos.
Design unique, story-specific calls to action that blend smoothly into the final seconds for a seamless loop without repeating the opening hook or using generic save reminders.
Verify that characters, settings, and time periods depicted in visuals accurately reflect the specific details mentioned in the voiceover without appearing generic.

schwaechen: The middle section relies on a chronological list of dates (2013, 2014, 2016) which functions as predictable list filler and slows down the narrative drive. Fix this by replacing the timeline with the causal mechanism of their growth: explain how they signed aggressive long-term leases while pitching themselves as a high-tech platform.
story.besserer_hook: How did a company valued at $47 billion collapse into bankruptcy?

skript.beschreibung:
WeWork was founded in 2010 and raised $12.8 billion over ten years, with valuations as high as $47 billion. Its 2019 IPO filing revealed governance issues, and it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on November 6, 2023, then shrank its operations.
Clips: Pixabay

leicht: The money poured in. - Qualitative claim not directly supported by the source; the source provides financing amounts but does not use this phrasing.
Trouble showed early. - Vague statement with no explicit support in the source material.
But it didn't vanish. - Assertion about the company's existence lacks direct evidence in the source; the source mentions continued operations but does not phrase it this way.

belege.name: WeWork
belege.text:
WeWork Inc. is an American company headquartered in New York City that provides coworking spaces, including physical and virtual shared spaces, in approximately 600 buildings in 125 cities.
WeWork was founded in 2010 by Adam Neumann and Miguel McKelvey. Over the following 10 years, the company raised $12.8 billion in financing at valuations as high as $47 billion, mostly from the SoftBank Vision Fund, led by Masayoshi Son. In September 2019, the company filed documentation to become a public company and revealed issues with corporate governance. Investors forced both the cancellation of the IPO and the resignation of Neumann. The company went public via a merger with a SPAC instead in 2021, and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on November 6, 2023. As part of the bankruptcy reorganization, in 2024, Cupar Grimmond (an affiliate of Yardi Systems) acquired a 60% stake in the company, 20% was acquired by affiliates of SoftBank, and 20% was acquired by other investors. The company shrank its operations, selling all owned real estate and cancelling or amending hundreds of leases.


History: 

2008–2015: In May 2008, Adam Neumann and American Miguel McKelvey established GreenDesk, an "eco-friendly coworking space" in Brooklyn. In 2010, Neumann and McKelvey sold the business and founded WeWork, renting its first location in SoHo, Manhattan, which opened in April 2011. Manhattan real estate developer Joel Schreiber purchased a 33% interest in the company for $15 million.
In 2011, PepsiCo placed a few employees in the location, who acted as advisors to smaller WeWork member companies, making the location a startup incubator.
By 2013, WeWork customers included 350 startups such as Fitocracy and HackHands.
By 2014, WeWork was considered "the fastest-growing lessee of new office space in New York" and was on track to become "the fastest-growing lessee [lessor] of new space in America." WeWork investors as of 2014 included J.P. Morgan Chase & Co, T. Rowe Price, Wellington Management, Goldman Sachs, the President and Fellows of Harvard College, Benchmark, and Mortimer Zuckerman, former CEO of Boston Properties.
In February 2015, WeWork was named to Fast Company’s 50 Most Innovative Companies list. On June 1, 2015, Artie Minson, former chief financial officer of Time Warner Cable, joined the company as president and chief operating officer. In August 2015, the company acquired CASE, a real estate and construction technology company, in its first acquisition. According to its founder, the speed of the transaction damaged the organizational culture of CASE.


2016: In March 2016, WeWork raised $430 million in financing from Legend Holdings and Hony Capital, valuing the company at $16 billion. In June 2016, the company announced layoffs of 7% of its staff and implemented a temporary hiring freeze. In July 2016, WeWork fired and sued Joanna Strange, an employee who leaked information to the press that showed that WeWork would miss its financial goals. By October 2016, the company had raised $1.7 billion in private capital. In October 2016, WeWork announced plans to open a fourth location in Central Square, Cambridge, with space for 550 desks. WeWork opened offices in Boston's Leather District and Fort Point in 2014. It also announced plans to open a location in Lincoln Square in Bellevue, Washington.
In 2016, WeWork launched a separate but related co-living venture called WeLive in New York City and in Crystal City, Virginia, near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in the Washington metropolitan area. A third WeLive location in Seattle was planned in the new Third and Lenora building in 2020, but the lease was terminated in October 2019. In July 2021, WeWork terminated this business line.


2017: In April 2017, WeWork launched an online store for services and software for its members. In May 2017, WeWork opened a luxury health club at its Broad Street, Manhattan location. The space includes exercise equipment and a boxing area, general workout area, spa, and a yoga studio with fitness classes. In June 2017, in partnership with Embassy Group, WeWork India, led by then 25-year old Karan Virwani, son of the Embassy Group owner Jitu Virwani, opened its first space in Bangalore, India, named WeWork Galaxy, with capacity for 2,200 members. In July 2017, the company raised $760 million in a Series G financing round valuing the company at $20 billion. Also in July 2017, WeWork announced expansion plans into China, with US$500 million invested by SoftBank and Hony Capital. In August 2017, the company raised $4.4 billion from the SoftBank Vision Fund at a valuation of approximately $20 billion. In September 2017, WeWork expanded into Southeast Asia via the acquisition of Singapore-based SpaceMob, and it allocated $500 million to grow in Southeast Asia.
In October 2017, WeWork signed a contract to acquire the Lord & Taylor Building on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan from the Hudson's Bay Company for $850 million, with additional plans to invest over $450 million on a renovation. The deal also included the use of floors of certain HBC owned department stores in Germany, New York, Toronto, and Vancouver as WeWork's shared office workspaces. The transaction closed in February 2019. The building was sold to Amazon.com in March 2020 for $1.15 billion.
In October 2017, WeWork acquired Flatiron School, a coding school. It was sold in June 2020. In November 2017, WeWork invested in The Wing, a co-working space for women. It sold the stake in January 2020. Also in November 2017, WeWork acquired Meetup for approximately $156 million. It was sold at a loss in 2020. In the same month, WeWork invested in Wavegarden, which designs and manufactures artificial wave devices. In addition, during November 2017, WeWork announced that in the fall of 2018 it would launch WeGrow, a private school for children aged 3 through students in grade 4. The first permanent location was in WeWork's New York headquarters. In September 2019, Rebekah Neumann resigned as CEO of WeGrow. WeGrow closed at the end of the 2019 academic year. In December 2017, WeWork opened its first location in Singapore.


2018: 
In January 2018, students taking online university courses from 2U were given access to WeWork common spaces and meeting rooms. In December 2018, WeWork opened its first location on a college campus at the University of Maryland, College Park. In March 2018, WeWork raised over $400 million alongside Rhône Group, a private equity firm to start a fund to purchase properties directly. Also in March 2018, WeWork acquired Conductor. Conductor executives bought back the company from WeWork in December 2019. In April 2018, WeWork acquired Chinese coworking operator Naked Hub for $400 million. In May 2018, WeWork acquired MissionU, a self-styled college alternative, for $4 million in stock. MissionU was wound-down shortly afterwards and students were not charged tuition. Cash was returned from MissionU to its investors. Mission
